title: Unacademy's ₹50 Crore ESOP Buyback: What It Means for Employees
description: Unacademy's ₹50 crore ESOP buyback came at a valuation below its last round. What employees got, how the payout is taxed, and the lessons for ESOP holders.
quickAnswer: In February 2026, Unacademy co-founder Gaurav Munjal announced a ₹50 crore ESOP buyback to give employees liquidity.
Munjal said 8 employees could earn over ₹1 crore each, 17 over ₹50 lakh and 38 over ₹10 lakh.
He also said the buyback valuation was significantly lower than Unacademy's last fundraise, so employees sold below the peak price.
How each employee is taxed depends on the payment date and the route: before 1 April 2026 a company buyback was taxed as a deemed dividend; from 1 April 2026 it is capital gains.

sections.title: A ₹50 crore buyback, announced on X.
body: On 27 February 2026, Business Today reported that Unacademy had launched a ₹50 crore ESOP buyback programme. Co-founder Gaurav Munjal announced it on X and said the company would contact eligible employees over the following weeks.
Munjal also shared how the money would be spread: 8 employees were expected to receive more than ₹1 crore each, 17 more than ₹50 lakh and 38 more than ₹10 lakh.
The buyback came while Unacademy was restructuring. It was moving its offline centres to a franchise model, and acquisition talks with upGrad had ended without a deal on valuation.

sections.title: The buyback valuation was below the last round. Why that matters.
body: Munjal said the valuation used for the buyback was significantly lower than Unacademy's last fundraise. No figures were disclosed.

For employees, this is the uncomfortable truth about ESOPs: the price in the headline of a funding round is not the price you will get. A buyback is set at whatever the company and its board decide is fair today.

Munjal had also cautioned earlier that preference shareholders rank ahead of equity holders. Investors usually hold preference shares with a liquidation preference: in a sale or wind-down, they get their money back first. Employees hold ordinary equity, which is paid only from what is left.
So a buyback below the peak can still be a good outcome. It is cash now, at a known price, instead of a share of whatever remains later.
sections.warning: When a company's latest valuation is below an earlier round, the value of your options depends on the preference stack, not just the price per share. Ask HR how much preference capital ranks ahead of ordinary shares.

sections.title: The payment date decides how the payout is taxed.
body: India changed how buybacks are taxed on 1 April 2026, and a buyback announced in late February could be paid on either side of that date.

If the company bought back shares and paid between 1 October 2024 and 31 March 2026, the whole amount received was a deemed dividend, taxed at the employee's slab rate. Their cost could only be claimed as a capital loss.
If the payment was on or after 1 April 2026, the gain over the employee's cost is capital gains. Shares held for more than 24 months are taxed at 12.5%; shorter holdings at the slab rate.
If an employee surrendered unexercised options for cash instead of selling shares, the payout is salary either way, taxed at the slab rate with TDS.

sections.title: Same ₹50 lakh payout, a week apart, very different tax.
body: Illustrative numbers, not Unacademy's. An employee sells shares in a company buyback for ₹50,00,000. The shares' FMV when they exercised, which is their cost, was ₹10,00,000, and they have held them for more than 24 months.

Paid on 25 March 2026 (deemed dividend): the whole ₹50,00,000 is taxed at the slab rate. At 30% plus 4% cess, that is ₹15,60,000, before surcharge. The ₹10,00,000 cost becomes a capital loss they can only set off against other capital gains.
Paid on 6 April 2026 (capital gains): the gain is ₹50,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 = ₹40,00,000. At 12.5% plus 4% cess, that is ₹5,20,000, before surcharge.
The difference is about ₹10,40,000 on the same sale. If you are offered a buyback, the payment date is one of the first things to ask about.

sections.title: A reminder to check your exercise window.
body: The same report mentioned a one-time 30-day window for Unacademy's former employees to exercise their vested options.

Most ESOP schemes give leavers a limited time to exercise. Miss it and vested options usually lapse, which also means you cannot take part in a later buyback. If you have left a startup with vested options, find your exercise deadline in the ESOP scheme or your grant letter.

sections.title: One of many buybacks in 2026.
body: Unacademy was part of a wave. Indian startups bought back about $220 million of ESOPs in the first quarter of 2026, more than in all of 2024 or 2025. Others included BrowserStack, Innovaccer, CoinDCX and Cashfree Payments.

sections.title: What any ESOP holder can take from this.
body: Buybacks can happen in tough years too, not only after a big raise. When one is offered, a few questions decide most of what you take home.
bullets: Am I selling shares or surrendering options? The tax is very different.
When will I be paid? The payment date sets the tax rules.
How does the price compare with the last round and my grant's FMV?
How much preference capital ranks ahead of ordinary shares?
If I have left, is my exercise window still open?

personaViews.label: Employee
personaViews.value: Ask for the route, the price and the payment date in writing, then model the tax before you accept.

personaViews.label: Founder
personaViews.value: A buyback below the last round can still build trust if you explain the price and the preference stack honestly.

personaViews.label: HR
personaViews.value: Give each participant their exercise dates and FMVs, and tell them the expected payment date.

checklist: I know whether the offer buys shares or options.
I know the expected payment date.
I know my cost (FMV at exercise) for each tranche.
I understand how much preference capital ranks ahead of me.
If I have left, I know my exercise deadline.
mistakes: Valuing your ESOPs at the last round's headline price.
Ignoring the liquidation preference held by investors.
Assuming the tax rules from the announcement date apply, instead of the payment date.
Letting the exercise window lapse after leaving.
Treating an option surrender like a share sale for tax.

faq.question: How big was Unacademy's ESOP buyback?
faq.answer: ₹50 crore, announced by co-founder Gaurav Munjal in February 2026.

faq.question: How much did Unacademy employees get in the buyback?
faq.answer: Munjal said 8 employees could earn over ₹1 crore each, 17 over ₹50 lakh and 38 over ₹10 lakh.

faq.question: Was the Unacademy buyback at a lower valuation?
faq.answer: Yes. Munjal said the buyback valuation was significantly lower than the company's last fundraise. The figure was not disclosed.

faq.question: How is an ESOP buyback paid in March 2026 taxed?
faq.answer: If the company bought back shares and paid before 1 April 2026, the full amount was a deemed dividend taxed at the slab rate, with the cost allowed only as a capital loss.

faq.question: What is a liquidation preference?
faq.answer: A right, usually held by investors with preference shares, to be paid back before ordinary shareholders such as employees when a company is sold or wound up.
